opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, part of it was just my personality. I've always liked setting goals that feel a little bit crazy, because if you aim really high and fall short, you still end up somewhere pretty good. If you aim for something comfortable, you tend to get exactly that, and sometimes less.

But there was also a practical side. By that point I felt I already knew what I wanted to do. I had a clear direction for my research and the things I wanted to build, and the degree itself was more of a milestone than the destination. So I asked myself: if I already know where I'm going, why spend extra time just going through the motions? I'd rather compress the formal requirements and spend my energy on the work that actually excites me.

And I think there's something about deadlines that really changes how you work. When you give yourself a tight timeline, you're forced to prioritize ruthlessly. You stop polishing things that don't matter, you stop waiting for the perfect moment, and you just start shipping. A lot of what I learned during that period wasn't the course content. It was learning how to manage myself, how to focus, and how to say no to things.

Of course, it wasn't easy, and there were moments when I wondered whether I was being too ambitious. But even then, I felt that pushing myself that hard taught me what my limits actually were, and they were further out than I'd assumed. That's something I've carried with me ever since.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that aiming really high can still lead to a good outcome even if you fall short, while comfortable goals tend to yield less.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was mostly about time, and about what a PhD is actually for.

When I started at MIT, I was already working on Taichi. The core ideas were there, the first papers were coming out, and I could feel that the project had momentum. A PhD is supposed to produce a body of original work and prove you can do research independently. By the end of that first stretch, I felt I had already done the thing. Staying another three or four years just to satisfy the calendar didn't make sense to me.

The other part is that I had a very clear sense of what I wanted to do next. Taichi was growing into something bigger than a thesis chapter. There were real users, there was a community, and there was a question of whether this could become a company. That window doesn't stay open forever. If I spent four more years polishing, someone else would build it, or the opportunity would simply pass.

So I talked to my advisor, and I was lucky that he was supportive. The plan was concrete: finish the remaining pieces, write the thesis, defend. Having a one-year target forced me to be disciplined about what actually mattered and what was just nice-to-have. A lot of people drift in a PhD because there's no deadline. I gave myself one.

I won't pretend it wasn't stressful. There were nights when I thought I'd set an impossible goal. But I think setting ambitious, slightly uncomfortable goals is how you find out what you're capable of. If I'd aimed for three years, it would have taken three years.

r001.rationale: The response says ambitious goals help reveal what one is capable of and create discipline, but it does not say that setting a more ambitious goal can produce better outcomes even when the goal is not fully achieved.

astra-6.text: I think I wanted to give myself a clear deadline. When you’re doing research, there’s always another idea to explore, and it’s easy to keep going without deciding when you’re done. Setting a goal of graduating in one year would force me to prioritize: what do I really want to finish, and what can wait? It wasn’t just about finishing quickly. It was about staying focused and being ready to move on to the next stage.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that a one-year goal creates a deadline and helps prioritize, but does not say that setting more ambitious goals leads to better outcomes even when the goals are not fully achieved.

sol-6.1.text: I wanted to give myself a clear deadline. If I left the timeline open, there would always be another experiment to run or another idea to explore. Setting a one-year goal forced me to decide what really mattered and focus on finishing it. Graduating wasn’t the end goal; I wanted to move on and put what I’d learned into practice.

r001.rationale: The response says a one-year deadline helped focus and finish the work. It does not present more ambitious goals as a way to achieve better outcomes even when those goals are not fully met.
